Discovering and Developing New Drugs

New medicines rarely appear quickly. The journey from a promising compound to a licensed drug typically spans more than a decade. Many potential drugs are discovered by screening natural sources — historically, the painkiller aspirin originated from willow bark compounds, and the heart drug digitalis from foxglove plants. Today, pharmaceutical companies also synthesise new molecules in the laboratory and test them computationally before any biological testing begins.

Key Fact

Drug testing has three stages: (1) preclinical testing on cells, tissues and animals; (2) clinical trials on healthy volunteers then patients, using double-blind placebo-controlled design; (3) peer review and regulatory approval. Each stage must be passed before the next begins.

Stage 1 — Preclinical testing: The drug is tested on cell cultures and isolated tissues to assess toxicity and efficacy. If results are promising, it moves to animal testing, which examines dose, toxicity and pharmacokinetics (how the body processes the drug). Preclinical testing cannot predict all human responses, but it filters out the most dangerous compounds.

Stage 2 — Clinical trials: Phase I involves a small number of healthy volunteers to assess safety and find a safe dose range. Phase II involves patients with the target condition, testing for effectiveness and monitoring side effects at a larger scale. Phase III is a large-scale randomised controlled trial. Double-blind design is used: neither the patient nor the clinician knows who receives the active drug and who receives a placebo. This eliminates placebo effect and observer bias. Results are analysed statistically after the trial is unblinded.

Stage 3 — Peer review and approval: Trial results are submitted to regulatory bodies (such as the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency in the UK) and published in peer-reviewed journals. Independent scientists scrutinise the methodology and data before the drug is approved for prescribing.

Monoclonal Antibodies

Monoclonal antibodies are produced by fusing a lymphocyte (which makes a specific antibody but cannot divide indefinitely) with a myeloma cell (a tumour cell that divides without limit but does not make antibodies). The resulting hybridoma cell can both divide without limit and produce a single, specific antibody. Large quantities of identical antibodies are cultured and purified.

Key Fact

Monoclonal antibodies are used in: (1) pregnancy testing — detecting the hormone HCG in urine; (2) cancer diagnosis — binding to tumour antigens to reveal their location; (3) cancer therapy — delivering drugs or radioactive labels directly to tumour cells while sparing healthy tissue.

Pregnancy testing: Early pregnancy is signalled by the hormone human chorionic gonadotrophin (HCG). A home pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies specific to HCG. If HCG is present in the urine sample, the antibodies bind to it; this complex moves along the test strip and triggers a coloured indicator, giving a positive result. If no HCG is present, no complex forms and the result is negative.

Cancer treatment: Some cancer cells display specific antigens not found on healthy cells. Monoclonal antibodies engineered to bind those antigens can be attached to a chemotherapy drug or a radioactive label. When injected, the antibody ‘seeks out’ cancer cells and delivers the toxic payload directly, reducing the collateral damage to healthy tissue that traditional chemotherapy causes. This is sometimes called targeted or ‘magic bullet’ therapy.

Limitations: Producing monoclonal antibodies is expensive and technically complex. They can cause unwanted immune reactions in some patients, and finding a tumour antigen unique enough to target without affecting healthy cells is difficult. Their development has raised ethical questions, particularly around the use of mice to generate the initial lymphocytes.

Non-Communicable Diseases: BMI and Obesity

Body mass index (BMI) is a widely used measure to classify whether a person’s mass is in a healthy range for their height. It is calculated as:

$$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\text{height (m)}^2}$$

For adults, a BMI of 18.5–24.9 is generally considered healthy; 25–29.9 is classed as overweight; 30 or above is classed as obese. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnostic measure. It does not distinguish between fat mass and muscle mass, so it can misclassify very muscular individuals. Waist-to-hip ratio is an alternative measure that better reflects abdominal fat distribution and associated health risk.

The relationship between obesity and disease is a correlation, not a simple linear cause. Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some cancers and joint problems. However, not all obese individuals develop these conditions and some non-obese individuals do. Other variables — genetics, diet quality, activity level, socioeconomic status — interact with mass to determine health outcomes. Examiners expect students to distinguish between correlation and causation in data questions.

Cardiovascular Disease

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is one of the leading non-communicable causes of mortality. It is strongly associated with lifestyle risk factors: a diet high in saturated fat and salt, physical inactivity, smoking, obesity, high blood pressure and high blood cholesterol. Fatty deposits build up in the walls of the coronary arteries over time — this is called atherosclerosis — narrowing the lumen and restricting blood flow to the heart muscle.

Statins are drugs that reduce blood cholesterol by blocking the enzyme responsible for its synthesis in the liver. Lower cholesterol slows the build-up of fatty plaques in the arteries. Statins are taken daily, reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, but can cause side effects including muscle pain in some patients.

Stents are small metal mesh tubes inserted into a narrowed coronary artery during keyhole surgery to prop it open and restore blood flow. Stents provide immediate relief but do not prevent further plaque build-up in other vessels. Patients may need to take blood-thinning drugs after stent insertion.

More invasive options include coronary artery bypass surgery, where a healthy blood vessel from another part of the body is grafted to bypass the blocked section. In severe cases, an artificial or donor heart may be considered. All surgical interventions carry risk; lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, stopping smoking) remain the most effective primary prevention.

Key Fact

Statins lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting the enzyme that synthesises it in the liver — reducing the rate of plaque formation in arteries. Stents mechanically prop open narrowed arteries. Both reduce cardiovascular risk but neither reverses existing damage; lifestyle change prevents further progression.

Levels of Organisation in Ecosystems

Living things exist in a hierarchy of levels. An ecosystem is the largest level: it includes all the organisms in a habitat together with the non-living factors that affect them. Within the ecosystem, a community is made up of all the different species. A population is all the individuals of a single species.

Abiotic factors include light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH, mineral content, wind speed and availability of water. Biotic factors include food availability, predators, pathogens and competition. Interactions between abiotic and biotic factors determine which species can live in a habitat and in what numbers.

Organisms in a community can interact in different ways. Parasitism is where one organism benefits at the direct expense of another (e.g. fleas living on a dog). Mutualism is where both organisms benefit (e.g. oxpecker birds eating insects on cattle — the bird gets food, the cattle lose parasites).

Key Fact

Ecosystem → community (all species) → population (one species). Abiotic factors are non-living; biotic factors are living. Stable communities maintain balanced populations when abiotic and biotic factors are in equilibrium.

Sampling Techniques: Quadrats and Belt Transects

To investigate the distribution and abundance of organisms in a habitat, scientists use systematic sampling methods. A quadrat is a square frame placed at random (using random numbers to generate coordinates) in the habitat. The number or percentage cover of organisms inside is recorded. Multiple quadrats are used to give a representative mean.

A belt transect is used to investigate how species distribution changes along an environmental gradient — for example, from the edge of a woodland into open grassland, or up a rocky shore. Quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the transect line and species recorded at each position. This reveals zonation: changes in species distribution that correlate with the changing abiotic conditions.

Key Fact

Quadrats are used to estimate the abundance or percentage cover of species in a habitat, using random sampling. Belt transects are used when species distribution is expected to change along a gradient. Both are core practical techniques — examiners test apparatus, method, control variables and how data are analysed.

Trophic Levels and Energy Transfer

Energy enters ecosystems through photosynthesis in producers (plants and algae). Energy then passes through organisms at each trophic level as organisms eat each other. At each transfer, most energy is lost as heat from respiration, through waste materials and in parts of organisms that are not eaten. Typically, only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next — this limits food chains to around four or five levels.

Energy transfer efficiency can be calculated: $$\text{efficiency (\%)} = \frac{\text{energy transferred to next level}}{\text{energy available at current level}} \times 100$$ For example, if 10,000 kJ is available at trophic level 1 (producers) and only 1,000 kJ reaches trophic level 2 (primary consumers), the transfer efficiency is 10%. This low efficiency is why fish farming (raising fish in enclosures and controlling feeding) can be more energy-efficient than wild fishing: energy is not lost through the fish swimming large distances or maintaining body temperature in cold water.

Non-indigenous (invasive) species introduced into a new habitat can outcompete native species, leading to population declines or local extinction. For example, grey squirrels introduced to the UK outcompete red squirrels for food and carry a disease (squirrelpox) to which red squirrels have no immunity.

Eutrophication occurs when excess fertiliser (nitrates and phosphates) runs off agricultural land into rivers and lakes. This causes rapid algal growth (an algal bloom), which blocks light from underwater plants, causing them to die. Decomposers break down the dead plant matter, consuming dissolved oxygen. The low oxygen levels kill fish and other aquatic organisms, reducing biodiversity.

Biodiversity and Food Security

Biodiversity refers to the variety of different species in an ecosystem. High biodiversity means ecosystems are more stable and resilient — if one species declines, others can take over some of its roles. Human activities — deforestation, pollution, overexploitation of natural resources — are driving a significant loss of biodiversity worldwide.

Strategies to maintain biodiversity include habitat protection and restoration, reforestation (replanting trees where forests have been cleared), wildlife breeding programmes for endangered species, and seed banks that preserve plant genetic diversity. Maintaining biodiversity also supports food security by preserving the genetic diversity of crop species and the wild species that act as pollinators and pest controllers.

Food security means that people have reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food. Threats include growing global population, changes in climate affecting crop yields, spread of new crop diseases, and limited freshwater supplies. Solutions include developing drought-resistant crop varieties through selective breeding or genetic technology, reducing food waste and improving the efficiency of food production systems.

The Carbon Cycle and the Water Cycle

Carbon is constantly cycled through the environment. Producers remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis, incorporating it into organic molecules. Animals eat producers and use carbon in their own bodies. When organisms respire, carbon is returned to the atmosphere as CO2. When organisms die, decomposers break down dead organic matter through respiration and decay, releasing CO2 back into the atmosphere. Combustion of fossil fuels is an additional pathway that returns carbon stored over millions of years to the atmosphere in a short time.

The water cycle describes the continuous movement of water between the atmosphere, land and living organisms. Water evaporates from oceans, lakes and soil; plants release water vapour through transpiration. Water vapour rises and condenses to form clouds, then falls as precipitation. Run-off and rivers return water to the sea. Desalination can supplement freshwater supplies in arid regions but requires significant energy input.

What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction measures how quickly a chemical reaction proceeds. It is calculated using:

$$\text{rate of reaction} = \frac{\text{quantity of reactant used or product formed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

The ‘quantity’ can be measured as mass (g), volume of gas (cm3), or by monitoring a colour change. The four main factors that affect rate are: temperature, concentration (or gas pressure), surface area of solids, and the use of a catalyst.

Key Fact

Rate of reaction increases with: higher temperature, greater concentration (or pressure for gases), greater surface area, and the presence of a catalyst. It can be measured by: collecting gas produced, monitoring mass loss, or timing a colour change.

Collision Theory

Collision theory explains why these factors affect rate. For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with each other and that collision must have enough energy to overcome the activation energy. Any change that increases the frequency of successful collisions increases the rate.

Temperature: higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. Even a small temperature rise can dramatically increase rate.

Concentration / Pressure: a higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so particles are closer together and collide more often. For gases, increasing pressure has the same effect — it compresses the gas and raises particle density.

Surface area: breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface for reactant particles to collide with. The total volume of solid is unchanged but more of it is accessible, so collisions are more frequent.

Catalyst: provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. At any given temperature, a larger fraction of collisions now have enough energy to react, so the rate increases. The catalyst is not consumed.

Core Practical — Measuring Rates of Reaction

Your course includes a core practical investigating how factors affect the rate of reaction. Two standard methods are used:

Marble chips (calcium carbonate) react with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide gas:

$$CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2$$

Rate is measured by collecting the gas in a gas syringe and recording the volume every 30 seconds. The independent variable (e.g. concentration of acid, or surface area of chips) is changed; the dependent variable is the volume of CO2 produced over time. Control variables include: mass of marble chips, temperature, total volume of solution.

The initial gradient of a volume-vs-time graph gives the initial rate. Steeper gradients indicate faster rates. Each experiment should be repeated to check reproducibility and calculate a mean.

When sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, a yellow precipitate of sulfur forms:

$$Na_2S_2O_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow 2NaCl + H_2O + SO_2 + S$$

Rate is measured by placing the flask over a cross drawn on white paper and timing how long it takes for the cross to disappear as the sulfur cloud builds up. A shorter time means a faster rate. The independent variable is concentration (or temperature); the dependent variable is time for cross to disappear. Control variables: volume of solutions, room temperature, the same cross viewed from the same height.

Rate can then be expressed as \(\frac{1}{\text{time}}\) — this makes comparison easier as a larger value corresponds to a faster rate.

Key Fact

Both core practical methods require clear identification of: independent variable (what you change), dependent variable (what you measure), and control variables (everything else kept constant). Examiners look for repeats and a method of calculating rate from collected data.

Interpreting Rate Graphs

A graph of product formed against time produces a curve that starts steep and levels off as reactants are used up. The steeper the initial gradient, the faster the initial rate. When the line is horizontal, the reaction has stopped. Comparing two experiments on the same axes, the one with the steeper initial gradient has the faster rate — caused by higher temperature, greater concentration, greater surface area, or the presence of a catalyst.

For calculation questions, if rate is defined as 1/time, a shorter time means a faster rate. When drawing graphs of volume of gas against time, the steeper the initial gradient, the faster the rate. Catalysts and higher temperatures both produce steeper gradients without changing the final total volume of product obtained at completion, because the same amount of reactant is consumed in both cases.
